clinicalPearls: A phototoxic (not allergic) reaction that occurs when skin contaminated with plant furocoumarins (psoralens) is subsequently exposed to ultraviolet A light
Common sources include limes and other citrus, celery, parsnip, figs and giant hogweed, and the classic 'margarita' pattern follows handling limes in the sun
The eruption has a characteristic streaky, bizarre or drip-like configuration that mirrors where the plant juice ran or was smeared on the skin
There is an acute phase of erythema and blistering within a day or two of exposure, followed by striking, often long-lasting post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation
Because it is phototoxic, it can affect anyone given sufficient furocoumarin and ultraviolet A, and it does not require prior sensitisation
Handprint-shaped marks on a child, for example from an adult with lime or fruit juice on their hands, can be mistaken for non-accidental injury or bruising
Management is largely supportive with skin cleansing, treatment of the acute reaction, sun avoidance of affected areas and reassurance that the pigmentation fades slowly
reference.pathophysiology: Phytophotodermatitis is a phototoxic reaction in which furocoumarins (psoralens) transferred to the skin from plants absorb ultraviolet A radiation and, in the excited state, form covalent adducts with DNA and damage cell membranes, causing direct keratinocyte injury, inflammation and blistering. This is the same class of psoralen-plus-ultraviolet-A photochemical reaction exploited therapeutically in PUVA. Subsequent stimulation of melanocytes produces the characteristic and often prolonged post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation in the exact distribution of plant contact.
additionalDifferentials: Allergic contact dermatitis, including plant (Compositae) allergy
Non-accidental injury or bruising, particularly in children
additionalInvestigations: A careful history of plant, fruit or vegetable contact followed by sun exposure, and the site distribution
Recognition of the streaky or handprint pattern that strongly suggests the diagnosis
Photopatch testing only where a photoallergic contact dermatitis is being considered
Skin biopsy in atypical cases, showing phototoxic changes
Consideration of safeguarding assessment when handprint marks in a child raise concern
Review of medications and topical products for other photosensitisers if the cause is unclear
redFlags: Extensive blistering or involvement of a large body surface requiring burns-type care
Handprint or bruise-like marks in a child prompting a safeguarding assessment
Systemic photosensitivity suggesting a drug cause or an underlying porphyria
Ocular or mucosal involvement from plant sap contact
reference.prognosis: The acute phototoxic reaction settles over days to a couple of weeks, but the resulting post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation is often marked and can take many weeks to months to fade; the condition is entirely preventable by avoiding the combination of furocoumarin contact and sun exposure, and it does not recur without renewed exposure.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the streaky pigmentation as bruising and raising unwarranted safeguarding concerns, or conversely dismissing genuine concerns
Labelling it an allergic reaction and mismanaging it, when it is a phototoxic process affecting anyone
Failing to elicit the plant or fruit exposure history that explains the bizarre pattern
Not warning patients that the hyperpigmentation will persist long after the initial reaction resolves
references: British Photodermatology Group guidance on phototoxic and photosensitivity disorders
management: Wash residual plant furocoumarin from the skin promptly and remove the affected area from further sun exposure to halt the phototoxic reaction
Enforce photoprotection with sun avoidance, broad-spectrum UVA sunscreen and protective clothing
Treat the acute erythema and blistering with topical corticosteroids, cool compresses and simple wound care for blisters
Manage the prolonged post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation with reassurance and continued sun protection, considering topical depigmenting agents in selected cases
Provide analgesia and symptomatic care during the acute phase
Educate on prevention by avoiding the combination of furocoumarin contact (limes, citrus, celery, parsnip, figs, giant hogweed) with sunlight
Consider a safeguarding assessment when handprint-shaped marks in a child raise concern about non-accidental injury
